canonicalSources.title: Constitutional AI: Harmlessness from AI Feedback

topics.contribution: Used written principles plus model-generated critiques, revisions, and preference labels to train a less harmful assistant with substantially less direct harmfulness labeling.
topics.prerequisites: RLHF, supervised fine-tuning, reward models, and self-critique.
topics.readingLens: The constitution makes values more explicit but does not remove human choice. Humans still write principles, select models, design prompts, and decide evaluation.
topics.equation: Principles → critique/revision data → AI preferences → RL policy, with humans choosing the constitution.

problem: RLHF requires people to inspect and rank potentially harmful content at scale. It can also hide the normative basis of labels inside examples and instructions rather than expose a concise statement of principles.
Constitutional AI asks whether a model can supervise much of its own harmlessness training when guided by an explicit list of rules.
coreIdea: In the supervised phase, elicit a harmful response, ask the model to critique it against a sampled constitutional principle, and ask for a revised answer. Fine-tune on the revisions.
In the reinforcement phase, a model compares response pairs according to the constitution. Those AI preferences train a reward model, and reinforcement learning optimizes the assistant against it.
mechanism: A red-team prompt produces an initial answer. A critique prompt names a principle and identifies violations. A revision prompt improves the answer. Repeating across principles creates harmlessness demonstrations.
For RLAIF, response pairs are evaluated by a preference model prompted with principles. Helpfulness feedback can still come from humans, balancing refusal with useful engagement.
technical: The method changes the data-generation process more than the base architecture. Chain-of-thought-style critiques provide a richer supervision trace than a binary safe/unsafe label.

Principle sampling, critique quality, evaluator bias, and reward-model generalization determine the learned behavior. Self-supervision is not independent when actor and evaluator share training data or blind spots.
evidence: The paper reported a Pareto improvement in helpfulness and harmlessness over RLHF baselines at sufficient scale, along with more transparent explanations for refusals. Scaling improved the model’s ability to apply principles.
Evaluation still depends on model and human judgments. Results support the pipeline under the selected constitution, not universal moral agreement.
impact: Constitutional AI made written policy a first-class model-training artifact and popularized RLAIF. It influenced later self-improvement, critique, and scalable-oversight research.
For organizations, it suggests a maintainable link between policy language, training data, automated evaluation, and observed behavior.
engineering: Version every principle with examples, scope, rationale, conflicts, and evaluation cases. Test whether revisions are genuinely safer or merely more verbose and evasive.
Use independent checks for high-risk domains. A model judging a related model can share systematic errors, so constitutional supervision should complement external evidence and tool-level controls.
limits: A constitution can be incomplete, culturally narrow, internally inconsistent, or gamed. Model-generated preferences may amplify shared blind spots and give an appearance of objectivity.
Harmlessness can overproduce refusals, while explanations can sound principled without reflecting the actual causal process. Production safety still needs monitoring and governance.
connections: Constitutional AI modifies InstructGPT’s feedback source while retaining preference modeling and RL. Self-Instruct similarly uses model-generated data, but targets task diversity rather than a safety constitution.
takeaways: Written principles make the supervision target more inspectable.
Models can generate critiques and revisions for training.
AI feedback reduces but does not remove human value choices.
Self-evaluation can share the actor model’s blind spots.
Helpful and harmless behavior must be balanced.
Policy versioning should connect to evals and deployment controls.

topics.title: Self-Instruct: Aligning Language Models with Self-Generated Instructions
topics.authors: Yizhong Wang, Yeganeh Kordi, Swaroop Mishra, Alisa Liu, Noah A. Smith, Daniel Khashabi, Hannaneh Hajishirzi
topics.organization: University of Washington and Allen Institute for AI

canonicalSources.title: Self-Instruct: Aligning Language Models with Self-Generated Instructions

topics.contribution: Bootstrapped instruction-following data by asking a language model to generate new tasks, inputs, and outputs, then filtering and fine-tuning on the synthetic collection.
topics.prerequisites: Instruction tuning, few-shot prompting, semantic similarity, and dataset filtering.
topics.readingLens: Synthetic data can scale coverage but inherits the teacher’s biases and errors. The filtering pipeline is the central engineering asset.
topics.equation: Seed tasks → generate instruction/input/output → filter → fine-tune → evaluate.

problem: Instruction-tuned models need diverse demonstrations, but manually authoring many tasks is expensive. Existing public NLP datasets cover a limited set of formats and may not resemble natural requests.
The paper asks whether a capable base model can create enough useful instruction data to improve itself through supervised fine-tuning.
coreIdea: Begin with a small human-written seed set. Prompt a teacher model to invent new instructions and decide whether they require an input. Generate instances and answers, remove invalid or near-duplicate tasks, and fine-tune a base model on what remains.
The learner is not discovering truth autonomously; it is distilling and reorganizing behaviors already accessible to the teacher, with filters shaping the result.
mechanism: Sample seed examples as in-context demonstrations. Generate batches of tasks, classify their input structure, create input-output instances, and apply heuristic and semantic-similarity filters.
Mix synthetic data with seed tasks, fine-tune, and evaluate on held-out instructions using humans and automatic metrics.
technical: ROUGE-L similarity was used to reject instructions too close to existing tasks, while blacklist and formatting checks removed malformed generations. The final dataset contained tens of thousands of instructions.
Quality compounds multiplicatively: task validity, input relevance, answer correctness, diversity, and filtering precision all affect the learner.
evidence: The resulting model substantially improved over the untuned GPT-3 base on the paper’s instruction evaluation and approached the behavior of models trained with proprietary instruction data.
The teacher was a strong proprietary model, so the result does not show a weak model can bootstrap arbitrarily beyond its source capability. Human evaluation remained necessary.
impact: Self-Instruct launched a broad family of synthetic instruction datasets and teacher-student tuning recipes. It lowered the cost of creating domain and language variants.
It also shifted bottlenecks toward data governance, decontamination, evaluator design, and knowing when synthetic volume merely repeats one model’s style.
engineering: Build validators per task family: executable tests for code, schema checks for extraction, citations for factual QA, and adversarial filters for policy. Similarity filtering alone does not ensure correctness.
Keep synthetic origin and teacher version in metadata. Mix human or grounded examples to prevent stylistic collapse and audit important slices manually.
limits: Synthetic tasks inherit teacher hallucinations, cultural assumptions, and blind spots. Heuristic diversity can be superficial, and generated answers may be impossible to verify.
Repeated self-training risks model collapse or narrowed distributions. The paper improves instruction following but does not provide a general self-improvement guarantee.
connections: Self-Instruct shares model-generated supervision with Constitutional AI but optimizes task coverage. DPO and ORPO later learn preferences over responses rather than only imitating synthetic targets.
takeaways: A small seed set can expand into a large instruction dataset.
Generation and filtering are equally important.
Synthetic volume does not guarantee factual quality.
Teacher lineage should remain visible.
Task-specific validators are stronger than generic similarity filters.
Human and grounded data still provide essential anchors.

topics.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model
topics.authors: Rafael Rafailov, Archit Sharma, Eric Mitchell, Stefano Ermon, Christopher D. Manning, Chelsea Finn

canonicalSources.title: Direct Preference Optimization: Your Language Model is Secretly a Reward Model

topics.contribution: Derived a direct classification loss for preference alignment, avoiding an explicit reward model and online reinforcement-learning loop.
topics.prerequisites: RLHF, KL-regularized policy optimization, pairwise logistic loss, and log probabilities.
topics.readingLens: DPO simplifies optimization, not preference data. Dataset quality, reference policy, sampling coverage, and β still determine behavior.
topics.equation: L_DPO = −log σ(β[(log π(yw|x)−log πref(yw|x))−(log π(yl|x)−log πref(yl|x))])

problem: Classic RLHF trains a reward model and then runs PPO, creating multiple models, sampling infrastructure, and instability. Yet the final objective is a KL-constrained preference policy.
DPO asks whether the optimal policy-reward relationship can eliminate the intermediate reward-model fitting and RL machinery.
coreIdea: Under the KL-regularized reward-maximization objective, reward can be expressed through the log ratio between the target policy and a reference policy. Substitute that relationship into the pairwise preference likelihood.
The result is a supervised loss that raises the preferred answer’s relative log probability and lowers the rejected answer’s, while anchoring changes to the reference.
mechanism: Collect prompt, chosen response, and rejected response triples. Freeze a reference model, usually the SFT checkpoint. Compute policy and reference log probabilities for both responses.
Apply the logistic DPO loss and update only the policy. Evaluate preference win rates and divergence, then tune β to trade alignment strength against reference proximity.
technical: DPO is equivalent to fitting an implicit reward represented by policy log ratios under the derivation’s assumptions. Sequence log probabilities require careful masking and length handling.
β controls effective KL strength. Label noise and response-pair coverage matter because offline optimization cannot query new examples where the policy drifts.
evidence: The paper reported that DPO matched or exceeded PPO-based methods on sentiment control, summarization, and dialogue while being simpler and more stable to train.
Results use selected datasets and evaluator models or humans. They show an effective alternative in those settings, not dominance over every online RL method.
impact: DPO became a standard post-training baseline because it fits ordinary fine-tuning infrastructure and removes reward-model/PPO operations. Many later objectives are modifications of its reference and preference terms.
Its popularity also made preference-data curation, pair difficulty, and offline evaluation more visible bottlenecks.
engineering: Compute log probabilities with identical tokenization and masks for policy and reference. Monitor chosen/rejected margins, KL, response length, and held-out win rate to catch pathological shortcuts.
Keep a clean SFT anchor and representative preference pairs. DPO cannot learn behavior absent from the dataset and can overfit annotator artifacts.
limits: The derivation assumes a reward/preference model form and sufficient offline coverage. Fixed datasets do not adapt when the policy finds new failure regions.
Reference dependence and β tuning can limit improvement. Preference likelihood is still a proxy and may reward style over factual correctness.
connections: DPO simplifies InstructGPT’s RL stage. ORPO removes the separate reference model and combines supervised likelihood with an odds-ratio penalty. GRPO returns to online sampled rewards without a learned critic.
takeaways: DPO turns preference alignment into a supervised pairwise loss.
The reference policy supplies the behavioral anchor.
No explicit reward model or PPO loop is required.
β controls the strength of deviation.
Offline pair coverage limits what can be learned.
Preference wins are not equivalent to factual correctness.

topics.title: ORPO: Monolithic Preference Optimization without Reference Model
topics.authors: Jiwoo Hong, Noah Lee, James Thorne

canonicalSources.title: ORPO: Monolithic Preference Optimization without Reference Model

topics.contribution: Combined supervised instruction tuning and preference separation in one reference-free objective using an odds-ratio penalty.
topics.prerequisites: SFT, sequence likelihood, preference pairs, odds, and DPO.
topics.readingLens: ORPO’s operational value is a one-stage reference-free pipeline. Inspect whether simplicity changes memory, tuning sensitivity, or output length on your dataset.
topics.equation: L_ORPO = L_SFT(chosen) + λ × preference odds-ratio loss(chosen, rejected)

problem: Many alignment pipelines first run SFT and then optimize preferences with a frozen reference model. This creates stages, extra model memory, and hyperparameter interactions.
ORPO asks whether the chosen response can provide the supervised target while an additional term directly separates it from a rejected response in the same update.
coreIdea: Maximize the likelihood of the preferred response as in instruction tuning, then penalize the odds of the rejected response relative to the preferred response. No separate reference checkpoint participates in the loss.
The supervised term keeps the model learning the desired answer, while the odds-ratio term introduces contrast.
mechanism: Prepare prompt, chosen, and rejected triples. Run the policy on both responses. Compute standard negative log likelihood for the chosen sequence and a relative odds penalty between response probabilities.
Weight the preference term by λ, update one model, and evaluate both task quality and preference win rate.
technical: Odds transform probability through p/(1−p), making the contrast sensitive to confidence. Implementations usually work in log space for numerical stability and aggregate token probabilities into a sequence score.
Without a reference model, the SFT loss becomes the principal anchor. λ and response-length normalization determine how strongly rejection separation shapes the model.
evidence: The paper reported competitive or stronger results than several SFT and preference baselines across model sizes and dialogue evaluations while using a simpler monolithic pipeline.
Model-judged comparisons and selected instruction datasets limit generalization. Independent replications should match preprocessing and length treatment.
impact: ORPO became part of the growing family of reference-free preference objectives and showed that alignment pipelines can be simplified further than DPO.
It is useful when memory or operational complexity makes a frozen reference model expensive, but simplicity alone does not select the right preference data.
engineering: Log chosen likelihood, preference margin, length, KL against the original base model, and held-out capability. A reference-free objective can still drift substantially.
Run controlled comparisons with SFT and DPO under identical data and token budgets. Objective names matter less than stable gains on representative evals.
limits: The odds-ratio formulation introduces its own tuning sensitivity and assumptions. Reference-free does not mean unconstrained behavior is safe.
Evidence is newer and narrower than long-established supervised training. Preference noise, evaluator bias, and offline coverage remain unchanged.
connections: ORPO starts from DPO’s direct preference framing but removes the reference and merges SFT. GRPO instead samples groups online and normalizes scalar rewards.
takeaways: ORPO performs instruction and preference tuning in one stage.
The chosen answer supplies the supervised anchor.
No frozen reference model is required.
An odds-ratio term separates chosen and rejected responses.
Reference-free training still needs drift monitoring.
Dataset and evaluation quality dominate objective branding.

topics.title: DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models
topics.authors: Zhihong Shao, Peiyi Wang, Qihao Zhu, Runxin Xu, Junxiao Song, Xiao Bi, Haowei Zhang, Mingchuan Zhang, Y. K. Li, Y. Wu, Daya Guo

canonicalSources.title: DeepSeekMath: Pushing the Limits of Mathematical Reasoning in Open Language Models

topics.contribution: Introduced Group Relative Policy Optimization in DeepSeekMath, using rewards normalized across sampled answer groups to train reasoning without a separate value model.
topics.prerequisites: Policy gradients, PPO, KL penalties, reward functions, and sampled reasoning outputs.
topics.readingLens: GRPO saves critic memory and works well with verifiable rewards, but relative normalization and repeated sampling change variance, cost, and failure modes.
topics.equation: advantage_i = (reward_i − mean(group rewards)) / std(group rewards)

problem: PPO-style RLHF uses a value model to estimate advantages, adding memory and training complexity comparable to another large network. Mathematical reasoning offers outcome rewards that can score sampled answers directly.
DeepSeekMath sought an efficient reinforcement-learning method that could improve reasoning while avoiding a separate critic.
coreIdea: For each prompt, sample a group of responses from the current or old policy. Score each response, then normalize rewards within the group to create relative advantages. Optimize a clipped policy objective with a KL regularizer.
Each answer is judged against its siblings rather than an absolute learned value baseline. This makes group diversity and reward quality central.
mechanism: Sample G completions for one problem. Apply rule-based or learned rewards. Compute group mean and standard deviation, assign normalized advantages, and update token probabilities with a PPO-like clipped ratio.
Repeat with fresh groups as the policy improves. A reference model or analytic KL term limits destructive drift.
technical: Removing the critic reduces memory, but sampling several long completions increases inference cost. When all group rewards are equal, normalized advantage carries little information; near-zero variance needs stable handling.
Outcome rewards can reinforce correct final answers while leaving flawed hidden reasoning unexamined. Process rewards offer denser signals but require more reliable labels.
evidence: DeepSeekMath reported large gains on mathematical benchmarks after continued pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, and GRPO. The full result cannot be attributed to GRPO alone because data and training stages interact.
Later systems expanded GRPO’s visibility, but those results are subsequent evidence and should not be retroactively assigned to the original paper.
impact: GRPO became a major method for reasoning-model post-training because it combines online exploration, verifiable rewards, and lower critic memory.
It shifted infrastructure toward high-throughput generation, grouped rollout storage, reward sandboxes, and careful policy-version control.
engineering: Use deterministic verifiers where possible and defend them against formatting hacks. Record prompt, policy checkpoint, samples, reward components, and group statistics for every rollout.
Track diversity and reward saturation. If all samples converge to one pattern, group-relative learning weakens and can amplify brittle strategies.
limits: Relative reward does not tell whether an entire group is good; it only ranks within the group. Weak or hackable verifiers can optimize incorrect behavior confidently.
Online sampling is expensive, and clipping/KL choices remain sensitive. Mathematical correctness provides unusually clean rewards that many business domains lack.
connections: GRPO contrasts with offline DPO and ORPO. Chain-of-Thought supplies reasoning traces, while Test-Time Scaling uses extra inference rather than weight updates to select better answers.
takeaways: GRPO replaces the learned critic with group-relative reward baselines.
Several responses must be sampled for each prompt.
Verifiable rewards make the method especially useful for math and code.
No critic does not mean low total compute.
Equal or hacked rewards provide weak learning signal.
Attribute DeepSeekMath gains to the full pipeline, not one objective.

topics.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models
topics.authors: Edward J. Hu, Yelong Shen, Phillip Wallis, Zeyuan Allen-Zhu, Yuanzhi Li, Shean Wang, Lu Wang, Weizhu Chen

canonicalSources.title: LoRA: Low-Rank Adaptation of Large Language Models

topics.contribution: Made large-model adaptation cheaper by freezing pretrained weights and learning small low-rank update matrices inside selected linear layers.
topics.prerequisites: Linear layers, matrix rank, fine-tuning, and optimizer memory.
topics.readingLens: LoRA reduces trainable state and checkpoint size. It does not reduce the frozen model’s inference memory unless adapters are merged or the base is separately quantized.
topics.equation: W adapted = W₀ + ΔW, where ΔW = (α/r)BA and rank(BA) ≤ r.

problem: Full fine-tuning updates every parameter and stores gradients plus optimizer states, making each task replica expensive. Prompting avoids training but may not deliver stable domain behavior.
The paper hypothesizes that task adaptation lives in a low-dimensional subspace, so the full weight matrix need not move independently.
coreIdea: Freeze W₀ and insert two trainable matrices: A projects into rank r and B projects back. Their product supplies an additive weight update. Initialize so the adapter starts with zero effect.
Only adapter parameters and optimizer state are saved. At deployment, the product can be merged into W₀ with no additional layer latency.
mechanism: Choose target projections, commonly attention query/value or later all major linear layers. Insert low-rank branches, scale by α/r, and train only those parameters.
Store one adapter per task or user. Load dynamically or merge for dedicated deployment; preserve the exact base-model identity because an adapter is relative to it.
technical: For a d-by-k weight, LoRA trains r(d+k) values instead of dk. Savings depend on rank and targeted modules. Optimizer memory falls with trainable parameters, while forward activations and frozen weights still consume memory.
Rank is capacity, not a direct quality setting. Alpha, dropout, module selection, learning rate, and data often matter as much as r.
evidence: The paper reported quality comparable to or better than full fine-tuning on several GPT and RoBERTa tasks with dramatically fewer trainable parameters and smaller checkpoints.
The experiments support low-rank adaptation for those models and tasks; they do not prove every downstream update has the same intrinsic rank.
impact: LoRA became the default unit of lightweight model customization and enabled adapter hubs, per-customer variants, and rapid experimentation.
It also separated base-model governance from adaptation artifacts, creating new requirements for adapter provenance, compatibility, and composition.
engineering: Version base hash, target modules, rank, alpha, tokenizer, and training data with every adapter. Test adapter swapping and merged/unmerged numerical behavior.
Estimate total memory, not trainable parameters alone. Use QLoRA when the frozen base is the bottleneck, and benchmark merged versus dynamic serving.
limits: Too little rank or narrow module targeting can underfit. Multiple simultaneous adapters can add latency or interact unpredictably, and merging complicates rollback.
Adapters can still teach unsafe behavior or memorize data. Parameter efficiency is not a security boundary or evidence of model ownership.
connections: QLoRA combines LoRA with a 4-bit frozen base. LLaMA’s practical checkpoints drove broad LoRA adoption. DPO and other alignment objectives can train LoRA adapters instead of full weights.
takeaways: LoRA learns an additive low-rank weight update.
The pretrained matrix stays frozen.
Optimizer and checkpoint storage shrink dramatically.
Base-model inference memory remains unless separately compressed.
Adapter compatibility requires exact lineage.
Rank and target-module choices need evaluation.

topics.title: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs
topics.authors: Tim Dettmers, Artidoro Pagnoni, Ari Holtzman, Luke Zettlemoyer

canonicalSources.title: QLoRA: Efficient Finetuning of Quantized LLMs

topics.contribution: Enabled high-quality fine-tuning of very large models on a single GPU by backpropagating through a frozen 4-bit quantized base into LoRA adapters.
topics.prerequisites: LoRA, quantization, floating-point formats, and optimizer memory.
topics.readingLens: QLoRA quantizes the frozen storage path while preserving higher-precision computation. Do not describe it as ordinary 4-bit training of every model weight.
topics.equation: 4-bit frozen W → dequantize for compute → gradients update only LoRA A and B.

problem: LoRA shrinks trainable state, but the frozen base can still require tens or hundreds of gigabytes. Existing 4-bit quantization mainly targeted inference and could lose quality during adaptation.
QLoRA seeks to preserve 16-bit fine-tuning quality while fitting a 65B model on one 48GB GPU.
coreIdea: Store the base model in 4-bit NormalFloat, dequantize blocks during matrix multiplication, and route gradients through the operation into higher-precision LoRA adapters without updating quantized base values.
Double quantization compresses quantization constants, and paged optimizers use unified memory to handle transient activation spikes.
mechanism: Quantize pretrained weights blockwise into NF4 plus scales. Insert LoRA modules broadly. During forward/backward, dequantize weights to a compute dtype and train adapter parameters.
Tune on instruction data, save only adapters, and evaluate both benchmark performance and human preference.
technical: NF4 is designed around normally distributed pretrained weights. Double quantization quantizes scale constants themselves. Memory accounting includes quantized weights, scales, activations, adapters, gradients, and optimizer state.
Paged optimizers prevent some out-of-memory spikes but can introduce host-device traffic. Sequence length and batch size still dominate activation memory.
evidence: The paper fine-tuned a 65B model on one 48GB GPU and reported that QLoRA variants could match full 16-bit fine-tuning on evaluated tasks. The Guanaco models performed strongly in chatbot comparisons.
The paper also showed that data quality strongly affects results and that benchmark suites can disagree with human judgments.
impact: QLoRA democratized large-model experimentation and made quantized adapter tuning common in open-model workflows.
It emphasized end-to-end memory engineering rather than one headline bit width.
engineering: Confirm hardware support for compute dtype and kernels. Measure peak memory under the longest real sequence, not an average batch.
Keep quantization config with the adapter and test final serving in the actual inference format; training-time quantization and deployment quantization may differ.
limits: 4-bit storage reduces weight memory but not all activations, KV cache, or compute. Paging can slow training, and quality may vary across architectures or highly precise domains.
Human preference evaluations can reward style. A strong chatbot score does not prove factuality, safety, or domain correctness.
connections: QLoRA builds directly on LoRA and practical open bases such as LLaMA. KV-cache quantization later applies low precision to runtime state rather than frozen parameters.
takeaways: QLoRA trains adapters through a frozen 4-bit base.
NF4 targets pretrained weight distributions.
Double quantization compresses scale metadata.
Paged optimizers manage transient memory pressure.
Activations and cache still require memory.
Data quality can matter more than adapter size.

topics.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity
topics.authors: William Fedus, Barret Zoph, Noam Shazeer

canonicalSources.title: Switch Transformers: Scaling to Trillion Parameter Models with Simple and Efficient Sparsity

topics.contribution: Simplified sparse mixture-of-experts routing to one expert per token, scaling model capacity to a trillion parameters while keeping per-token computation comparatively bounded.
topics.prerequisites: Transformer feed-forward layers, sparse routing, distributed training, and load balancing.
topics.readingLens: MoE increases total parameters without activating all of them. Separate parameter capacity, FLOPs per token, communication, memory, and serving efficiency.
topics.equation: y = expert_argmax(router(x))(x), plus an auxiliary load-balancing loss.

problem: Dense models increase computation for every token as parameters grow. Earlier MoE systems offered sparse capacity but suffered from routing complexity, communication, instability, and expert imbalance.
Switch Transformer asks whether choosing only one expert per token can make sparsity simpler and more scalable.
coreIdea: Replace selected feed-forward layers with many expert feed-forward networks. A learned router assigns each token to its highest-probability expert; only that expert computes the transformation.
An auxiliary objective spreads tokens across experts, while capacity limits define how many tokens each expert accepts.
mechanism: Compute router logits for each token, select top-1 expert, dispatch tokens across devices, process each expert batch, and combine outputs back into sequence order.
If an expert exceeds capacity, overflow tokens may skip the expert through the residual path. Routing noise and load loss discourage collapse onto a few experts.
technical: Sparse activation decouples total parameter count from active compute, but all-to-all communication and expert memory remain. Capacity factor trades dropped tokens against padding and utilization.
The paper uses reduced precision carefully and reports techniques that stabilize router computation. Expert parallelism adds a new axis beyond data and tensor parallelism.
evidence: Switch models improved pretraining speed and downstream quality over dense T5 baselines at matched compute in the reported regime, including a trillion-parameter experiment.
Total parameter count can make headlines while hiding communication cost and inactive weights. Comparisons must match active FLOPs and hardware topology.
impact: Switch Transformer made sparse MoE a practical route to high-capacity language models and influenced later open and proprietary architectures.
It turned router health, expert utilization, and distributed all-to-all traffic into core training metrics.
engineering: Monitor tokens per expert, overflow rate, routing entropy, auxiliary loss, and per-device stragglers. Average utilization can hide individual overloaded experts.
Design serving around expert placement and batch mix. Sparse FLOPs do not guarantee low latency when requests activate scattered experts or memory bandwidth dominates.
limits: Top-1 routing may restrict combination capacity, and expert specialization can be fragile. Overflow drops useful computation; load balancing can fight task-optimal routing.
MoE checkpoints are large to store and communicate. Fine-tuning and serving require specialized kernels and topology-aware placement.
connections: DeepSeekMoE refines specialization with smaller experts and shared experts. GQA and inference methods target runtime cache rather than feed-forward parameter activation.
takeaways: MoE scales capacity separately from active FLOPs.
Switch routing chooses one expert per token.
Load balancing is necessary for usable distributed training.
Capacity limits create overflow trade-offs.
Communication can dominate theoretical compute savings.
Total parameters are not active parameters.

topics.title: DeepSeekMoE: Towards Ultimate Expert Specialization in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models
topics.authors: Damai Dai, Chengqi Deng, Chenggang Zhao, R. X. Xu, Huazuo Gao, Deli Chen, Jiashi Li, Wangding Zeng, Xingkai Yu, Y. Wu, Zhenda Xie, Y. K. Li, Panpan Huang, Fuli Luo, Chong Ruan, Zhifang Sui, Wenfeng Liang

canonicalSources.title: DeepSeekMoE: Towards Ultimate Expert Specialization in Mixture-of-Experts Language Models

topics.contribution: Improved MoE specialization through finer-grained routed experts plus always-active shared experts that capture common knowledge.
topics.prerequisites: Switch Transformer, top-k routing, expert parallelism, and capacity planning.
topics.readingLens: DeepSeekMoE changes expert granularity and knowledge allocation. Compare active parameters and training compute, not only total model size.
topics.equation: output = shared experts(x) + Σ selected fine-grained routed experts(x).

problem: Conventional MoE experts may each contain mixed knowledge because their feed-forward blocks are large, while several experts redundantly learn common patterns. That weakens specialization and wastes routed capacity.
The paper seeks more combinations of smaller experts while reserving shared computation for knowledge useful to every token.
coreIdea: Split standard experts into smaller units and activate more of them so the same active parameter budget can form many combinations. Add shared experts that process every token and absorb common knowledge.
A device-limited routing strategy and load balancing support distributed execution.
mechanism: Every token passes through shared experts. The router scores many fine-grained experts, selects a top-k subset, dispatches token representations, and sums weighted outputs.
Training jointly learns shared and specialized paths. Auxiliary routing terms and infrastructure keep expert traffic balanced.
technical: Fine-grained segmentation increases combinatorial specialization without necessarily increasing active parameters. Shared experts reduce pressure for every routed expert to relearn universal features.
More selected experts can increase dispatch complexity. Physical placement, network topology, and batch size determine whether theoretical sparsity produces throughput.
evidence: The paper reported that DeepSeekMoE models achieved quality comparable to denser or larger baselines with fewer active parameters and extended the design to a 145B model.
Ablations support shared experts and segmentation in the tested setup, but cross-family comparisons depend on data, tokens, and optimization.
impact: The architecture influenced subsequent DeepSeek models and the broader move toward explicit shared-versus-routed knowledge paths.
It reinforced active parameter count as a more useful inference measure than total parameter count, though still incomplete.
engineering: Log shared and routed contribution, expert occupancy, route stability by domain, and cross-device bytes. Route visualizations can reveal collapse or accidental domain silos.
Capacity-plan for the busiest expert and failure mode, not average activation. Serving may need expert replication for hot routes.
limits: Shared experts can become a dense bottleneck, while fine-grained routing adds coordination cost. Expert specialization is difficult to interpret and may shift during adaptation.
The design still needs large total storage and specialized distributed software. Sparse architecture does not remove data or alignment problems.
connections: DeepSeekMoE extends Switch Transformer’s sparse capacity. GRPO later appears in DeepSeekMath for post-training rather than pretraining architecture.
takeaways: Smaller experts create more routing combinations.
Shared experts capture common knowledge.
Active and total parameters must be reported separately.
Routing quality and network traffic are coupled.
Expert heat maps are essential observability.
Sparse models still need full alignment and data governance.

topics.title: Muon is Scalable for LLM Training
topics.authors: Jingyuan Liu, Jianlin Su, Xingcheng Yao, Zhejun Jiang, Guokun Lai, Yulun Du, Yidao Qin, Weixin Xu, Enzhe Lu, Junjie Yan, Yanru Chen, Huabin Zheng, Yibo Liu, Shaowei Liu, Bohong Yin, Weiran He, Han Zhu, Yuzhi Wang, Jianzhou Wang, Mengnan Dong, Zheng Zhang, Yongsheng Kang, Hao Zhang, Xinran Xu, Yutao Zhang, Yuxin Wu, Xinyu Zhou, Zhilin Yang

canonicalSources.title: Muon is Scalable for LLM Training

topics.contribution: Scaled the Muon matrix optimizer to language-model training by orthogonalizing momentum updates, adding weight decay, and calibrating update scale.
topics.prerequisites: Momentum optimization, matrix norms, Newton-Schulz iteration, AdamW, and distributed training.
topics.readingLens: Muon is newer evidence, not a universal AdamW replacement. Understand which parameters receive matrix updates and which remain on AdamW.
topics.equation: Muon update ≈ NewtonSchulz( momentum_matrix ), scaled per parameter and combined with weight decay.

problem: AdamW treats coordinates largely independently and keeps two moment estimates per parameter. Muon proposed geometry-aware updates for 2D weight matrices but had not been validated at large language-model scale.
Scaling requires stable weight decay, comparable update magnitude across differently shaped tensors, and efficient distributed orthogonalization.
coreIdea: Build momentum for each hidden weight matrix, then approximately orthogonalize that update with Newton-Schulz iterations. This gives singular directions more balanced update magnitude than raw momentum.
Use AdamW for embeddings, normalization, biases, and other non-matrix parameters. Add decoupled weight decay and a shape-aware scale so Muon works across model sizes.
mechanism: Compute gradients and momentum. Normalize the matrix, run several Newton-Schulz polynomial iterations using matrix multiplications, rescale the result, apply weight decay, and update the weight.
Shard or communicate updates with an implementation designed to avoid storing unnecessary full optimizer state.
technical: Orthogonalization is approximate and chosen because matrix multiplications map efficiently to accelerators. Update-scale calibration is critical: an orthogonal matrix’s entry and spectral statistics differ from Adam-normalized updates.
Muon reduces some optimizer-state requirements but adds matrix-multiplication work. Its cost depends on shape, parallelism, precision, and Newton-Schulz iteration count.
evidence: The paper’s scaling-law experiments reported about two-times compute efficiency versus AdamW under its compute-optimal setup and trained the Moonlight 3B/16B MoE model on 5.7T tokens.
Those results are substantial but come from one training stack and model family. Independent evidence across architectures and data regimes is still developing.
impact: Muon reopened optimizer design as a major LLM scaling lever and demonstrated that matrix geometry can be exploited with accelerator-friendly operations.
It also encouraged teams to benchmark training loss per FLOP rather than compare optimizer steps or wall time without systems context.
engineering: Start with a small scaling sweep and match total tokens, FLOPs, and data order against AdamW. Monitor update RMS, spectral norms, loss spikes, and per-parameter category.
Keep an explicit parameter partition: matrix weights on Muon, vectors and special parameters on AdamW. Validate distributed numerical agreement and checkpoint resume.
limits: Evidence is newer than AdamW’s broad deployment history. Orthogonalization assumptions fit matrix weights better than all parameter types, and kernel or communication overhead can erase gains.
Hyperparameter transfer, very small matrices, fine-tuning, multimodal models, and long-horizon stability need workload-specific validation.
connections: Muon complements scaling-law work by changing optimization efficiency rather than model/data allocation. It sits beside MoE methods that reduce active compute through architecture.
takeaways: Muon orthogonalizes momentum updates for matrix parameters.
Newton-Schulz uses accelerator-friendly matrix multiplications.
Weight decay and update scaling enabled larger runs.
Not every parameter should use Muon.
Compare loss per total FLOP under controlled data.
Current evidence is promising but still young.

topics.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
topics.authors: Tri Dao, Daniel Y. Fu, Stefano Ermon, Atri Rudra, Christopher Ré
topics.organization: Stanford University and University at Buffalo

canonicalSources.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness

topics.contribution: Reordered exact attention into SRAM-sized tiles, avoiding materialization of the full score matrix in high-bandwidth memory and improving speed plus memory usage.
topics.prerequisites: Attention, GPU memory hierarchy, tiling, softmax, and backward recomputation.
topics.readingLens: FlashAttention changes the algorithm’s IO schedule, not its mathematical attention result. Distinguish exactness from approximate sparse attention.
topics.equation: Tile Q,K,V; maintain running row max m and normalization ℓ for online softmax.

problem: Standard attention forms an N-by-N score matrix, writes it to GPU high-bandwidth memory, applies softmax, and reads it again. Those transfers dominate runtime before arithmetic capacity is exhausted.
Approximate attention reduces computation but may change outputs. The paper asks whether exact attention can move far fewer bytes.
coreIdea: Process query and key/value blocks that fit in fast on-chip SRAM. Compute partial scores and update a numerically stable online softmax plus output accumulator, never storing the complete attention matrix in HBM.
Backward recomputes score tiles from saved normalization statistics, trading cheap arithmetic for expensive memory traffic.
mechanism: Load a K/V tile, iterate over Q tiles, compute block scores, apply masks, update running maximum and denominator, and rescale the prior output accumulator before adding the new block.
Write only the final output and small softmax statistics. During backward, reconstruct each tile and accumulate gradients.
technical: Online softmax combines block statistics exactly: when a new block has a larger max, old sums and outputs are rescaled into the new exponent frame. This preserves numerical stability.
IO complexity depends on SRAM size and tiling. Causal masking skips useless regions, and kernel fusion avoids launches and intermediate buffers.
evidence: The paper reported substantial wall-clock speedups over PyTorch attention and much lower memory, enabling longer sequences on tested GPUs. End-to-end Transformer training also accelerated.
Speedups vary with GPU, dtype, head dimension, sequence length, dropout, and competing kernels. The theoretical IO advantage does not imply one fixed multiplier.
impact: FlashAttention made hardware-aware exact algorithms central to LLM engineering and enabled longer contexts without changing model semantics.
It became the foundation for production attention kernels and later improvements in work partitioning, decoding, and new accelerator generations.
engineering: Use framework-native fused scaled-dot-product attention when it dispatches to a supported kernel. Confirm masks, dropout, head size, and dtype do not trigger a slow fallback.
Benchmark end to end with realistic sequence distributions. A faster attention kernel may not dominate when feed-forward layers, communication, or data loading are the bottleneck.
limits: Dense arithmetic remains quadratic in sequence length even though memory is linearized. Very long contexts eventually hit compute and KV-cache limits.
Custom kernels are hardware- and shape-sensitive. Numerical differences from operation order are small but can complicate exact bitwise reproducibility.
connections: FlashAttention-2 improves parallel work partitioning. PagedAttention addresses cache allocation across requests, while MQA/GQA reduce cache size architecturally.
takeaways: FlashAttention is exact attention with a different IO schedule.
SRAM tiling avoids the full HBM score matrix.
Online softmax preserves stable normalization across tiles.
Backward recomputation saves memory.
Quadratic arithmetic remains.
Supported shapes and kernels determine actual speed.

topics.title: FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning
topics.authors: Tri Dao

canonicalSources.title: FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning

topics.contribution: Improved FlashAttention’s GPU utilization by reducing non-matrix work and repartitioning attention across thread blocks and warps.
topics.prerequisites: FlashAttention, GPU warps, occupancy, and matrix-multiply throughput.
topics.readingLens: The mathematics stays exact; the contribution is kernel work allocation. Read performance tables with GPU, sequence shape, and utilization in view.
topics.equation: Same exact attention; less rescaling overhead + better sequence and warp parallelism.

problem: FlashAttention moved fewer bytes but used only a fraction of peak GPU FLOPs. Small batch/head counts underutilized the device, while warp-level work partitioning caused shared-memory communication.
The second paper targets the gap between IO optimality and actual kernel utilization.
coreIdea: Reduce operations outside tensor-core matrix multiplication, parallelize a single head across sequence blocks when batch times heads is small, and divide work among warps to avoid unnecessary shared-memory exchange.
The attention result and online-softmax logic remain unchanged.
mechanism: Dispatch more thread blocks over query sequence length. Within a block, let warps share K/V while owning different Q slices, so each warp can compute its output without exchanging partial results.
Rearrange rescaling and masking to cut scalar FLOPs and improve occupancy.
technical: GPU throughput depends on keeping tensor cores busy and minimizing synchronization. The revised warp partition changes which data is shared and which accumulator remains private.
Backward has different dependency patterns from forward and requires its own partition strategy. Head dimensions up to 256 broaden useful model coverage.
evidence: The paper reported roughly two-times speed over FlashAttention on tested A100 workloads and reached a much larger fraction of theoretical peak throughput, with large end-to-end training gains.
These are kernel benchmarks under specified shapes and hardware. New GPU generations and vendor kernels can change the relative result.
impact: FlashAttention-2 became a common default attention implementation and demonstrated that algorithmic complexity alone is insufficient: scheduling and occupancy can double realized performance.
Its ideas informed subsequent variants optimized for longer context, decoding, and newer hardware.
engineering: Profile kernel dispatch rather than assuming a library name guarantees the fast path. Batch, heads, sequence lengths, causal mode, and head width determine occupancy.
Pin versions and test numerical plus performance regressions when upgrading CUDA, compiler, or framework. Kernel selection can change silently.
limits: Quadratic dense compute remains, and gains narrow when attention is not the workload bottleneck. Irregular masks or unsupported shapes may fall back.
Peak benchmark throughput does not include tokenization, communication, optimizer, or serving scheduler overhead.
connections: FlashAttention-2 is a systems refinement of FlashAttention. Speculative decoding attacks sequential token steps, while PagedAttention improves multi-request memory allocation.
takeaways: IO optimality does not guarantee high GPU utilization.
Warp partitioning determines synchronization cost.
More sequence parallelism helps small batch/head workloads.
The attention result remains exact.
Hardware and shape must accompany every speed claim.
Profile the actual dispatched kernel.

topics.title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
topics.authors: Yaniv Leviathan, Matan Kalman, Yossi Matias

canonicalSources.title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding
Accelerating Large Language Model Decoding with Speculative Sampling
canonicalSources.note: Companion primary paper included in the synthesis.

topics.contribution: Accelerated exact autoregressive sampling by letting a cheap draft propose several tokens and having the target model verify them in parallel without changing its output distribution.
topics.prerequisites: Autoregressive sampling, rejection sampling, probability distributions, and decode latency.
topics.readingLens: The method is lossless with respect to the target sampler under its acceptance correction. Speed depends on acceptance rate and target parallel efficiency.
topics.equation: Accept draft token with min(1, p_target(token)/p_draft(token)); sample correction on rejection.

problem: Large-model decoding is sequential: one expensive forward step usually produces one token, even when accelerator arithmetic is underutilized. Batching helps throughput but not single-request dependency depth.
A smaller model can predict likely continuations cheaply, but naively using its tokens changes quality.
coreIdea: Have a draft model generate a short token block autoregressively. Run the target model once over that block to obtain all target probabilities, then accept matching proposals with a rejection-sampling rule.
If several proposals are accepted, one target pass advances several tokens. A correction distribution on rejection preserves the target model’s sampling distribution.
mechanism: Draft γ tokens, evaluate them with the target in parallel, compare target and draft probabilities token by token, accept the prefix until the first rejection, sample a corrected token, and repeat.
When every proposal is accepted, also sample one additional target token from the final position to maximize progress.
technical: Correctness is distributional, not merely greedy agreement. The residual distribution is proportional to max(0, p−q) after rejection. Random-number handling and identical sampling settings matter.
Expected speedup grows with acceptance and the ratio between target-pass cost and draft cost. Longer speculation increases potential gain but wastes more work on early rejection.
evidence: The companion papers reported multiple-times decoding speedups across translation and language-model workloads while preserving the target distribution.
Results depend on model pair, hardware, batch size, sampling temperature, and implementation. High-throughput serving can have less idle target compute to exploit.
impact: Speculation created a broad design space: independent draft models, self-drafting heads, prompt lookup, tree proposals, and systems that adapt γ online.
It reframed small models as latency accelerators rather than only cheaper quality alternatives.
engineering: Measure accepted tokens per target pass, draft overhead, time to first token, inter-token latency, and end-to-end throughput. Tune speculation length by workload.
Keep tokenizer and vocabulary aligned or provide a proven mapping. Verify exact sampling with statistical tests, especially after kernel or quantization changes.
limits: Low acceptance can make the method slower. Domain shift, high temperature, creative tasks, and a weak draft reduce agreement.
Extra model weights consume memory, and correctness guarantees can break through approximate verification or mismatched sampling code.
connections: PagedAttention improves memory utilization across concurrent requests; speculation reduces target decode steps within a request. Test-Time Scaling intentionally spends extra inference compute for quality, the opposite optimization objective.
takeaways: A draft proposes multiple future tokens cheaply.
The target verifies proposals in one parallel pass.
Rejection sampling preserves the target distribution.
Acceptance rate determines useful speedup.
Draft cost and memory must be included.
Statistical correctness tests are essential.

topics.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention
topics.authors: Woosuk Kwon, Zhuohan Li, Siyuan Zhuang, Ying Sheng, Lianmin Zheng, Cody Hao Yu, Joseph E. Gonzalez, Hao Zhang, Ion Stoica

canonicalSources.title: Efficient Memory Management for Large Language Model Serving with PagedAttention

topics.contribution: Applied virtual-memory-style paging to KV cache and combined it with continuous batching, greatly improving serving throughput under variable request lengths.
topics.prerequisites: KV caching, GPU memory allocation, virtual memory, batching, and serving metrics.
topics.readingLens: PagedAttention is both a kernel abstraction and a serving-system design. Its gain comes from reducing fragmentation and enabling flexible scheduling.
topics.equation: Logical KV blocks map through a block table to non-contiguous physical GPU blocks.

problem: LLM servers reserve contiguous KV-cache memory for uncertain maximum sequence lengths. Variable prompts and outputs create internal waste, external fragmentation, and expensive reallocation.
Poor memory utilization reduces batch size and throughput even when compute is available. Sharing prefixes or beam-search cache is also awkward with contiguous buffers.
coreIdea: Divide each request’s KV cache into fixed-size logical blocks and map them to physical GPU blocks through a table, analogous to operating-system virtual memory pages.
PagedAttention kernels follow the mapping while continuous batching admits, pauses, and completes requests at token boundaries. Copy-on-write enables safe sharing.
mechanism: Allocate physical blocks only as tokens fill logical blocks. Store mappings per sequence. During attention, fetch K/V through the table. Reclaim blocks immediately when a request ends.
The scheduler mixes requests with different lengths and can swap or recompute state under pressure instead of reserving worst-case contiguous regions.
technical: Only the final block of a sequence has internal waste, bounded by block size. Non-contiguous storage requires a custom attention kernel and metadata lookup but avoids large memory copies.
Block size trades metadata and kernel efficiency against waste. Prefix sharing uses reference counts and copy-on-write when sequences diverge.
evidence: The vLLM paper reported two-to-four-times throughput improvements over tested FasterTransformer and Orca-style systems at comparable latency, with larger gains for long and variable sequences.
Serving results are workload distributions, not model-only constants. Modern baselines and kernels have evolved, so current systems require fresh benchmarking.
impact: PagedAttention made KV memory management a central serving abstraction and vLLM became a widely used open inference engine.
It enabled richer schedulers, prefix caching, distributed serving, and standardized OpenAI-compatible model endpoints.
engineering: Benchmark time to first token, inter-token latency, throughput, queue delay, and memory under the real prompt/output distribution. Average sequence length is insufficient.
Tune block size and scheduler limits together. Add admission control so a few very long requests cannot evict or starve interactive traffic.
limits: Paging does not shrink the logical KV cache; it allocates it more efficiently. Extremely long contexts still consume large memory, and block lookup adds kernel complexity.
Throughput optimization can harm tail latency without service-level objectives. Swap or recomputation policies introduce their own latency cliffs.
connections: MQA/GQA reduce cache bytes per token, while PagedAttention reduces allocation waste across requests. KV compression reduces precision or retained tokens; these methods can be combined.
takeaways: Contiguous KV reservation wastes accelerator memory.
Logical blocks decouple sequence growth from physical placement.
Continuous batching improves utilization at token boundaries.
Copy-on-write supports shared prefixes safely.
Paging manages but does not eliminate KV growth.
Serving quality requires latency and throughput together.

topics.title: H$_2$O: Heavy-Hitter Oracle for Efficient Generative Inference of Large Language Models
topics.authors: Zhenyu Zhang, Ying Sheng, Tianyi Zhou, Tianlong Chen, Lianmin Zheng, Ruisi Cai, Zhao Song, Yuandong Tian, Christopher Ré, Clark Barrett, Zhangyang Wang, Beidi Chen

canonicalSources.title: H$_2$O: Heavy-Hitter Oracle for Efficient Generative Inference of Large Language Models
KIVI: A Tuning-Free Asymmetric 2bit Quantization for KV Cache
canonicalSources.note: Companion primary paper included in the synthesis.

canonicalSources.title: SnapKV: LLM Knows What You are Looking for Before Generation
canonicalSources.note: Companion primary paper included in the synthesis.

topics.contribution: Synthesizes three complementary KV-cache levers: evict low-value tokens with H2O, quantize keys and values with KIVI, and select prompt positions with SnapKV.
topics.prerequisites: KV caching, attention heads, quantization, long-context evaluation, and serving workloads.
topics.readingLens: This is not one canonical paper. Each method saves a different dimension and accepts different quality, kernel, and workload risks.
topics.equation: KV bytes ≈ 2 × layers × retained tokens × KV heads × head dimension × bytes/value.

problem: Autoregressive attention stores keys and values for every retained token in every layer. Memory grows linearly with context, batch size, layers, KV heads, and precision, often limiting concurrency before model weights do.
Optimization can alter architecture, allocation, precision, token retention, or storage tier. This guide focuses on three papers that compress the existing cache.
coreIdea: H2O treats a small set of attention heavy hitters as important and combines them with recent tokens. KIVI uses asymmetric 2-bit quantization, exploiting different outlier patterns in keys and values. SnapKV observes attention near the prompt boundary to select positions likely to matter during generation.

The methods are complementary in principle, but their errors can compound. The correct design depends on whether the workload needs exact retrieval, broad summarization, long generation, or high concurrency.
mechanism: H2O scores historical tokens by accumulated attention and evicts low-value entries while preserving recency. KIVI quantizes keys per channel and values per token, retaining a small full-precision residual window. SnapKV pools attention votes across heads and keeps selected prompt clusters.
All methods require kernels and cache metadata that match their representation. Quality evaluation must target position, domain, and generation length.
technical: The cache equation shows independent multipliers. GQA reduces KV heads; low-bit methods reduce bytes per value; eviction/selection reduces retained tokens; paging reduces allocation waste; offload changes memory tier.
Attention importance is layer- and head-dependent. Quantization outliers differ between keys and values. A method that preserves perplexity may still fail exact needle retrieval.
evidence: H2O reported strong generation quality with a small heavy-hitter cache. KIVI reported near-lossless quality with a 2.6-times peak-memory reduction and higher throughput in tested systems. SnapKV reported large prompt-cache reductions with limited benchmark loss.
The papers use different models, tasks, baselines, and budgets; headline ratios should not be compared as one leaderboard.
impact: KV optimization became essential as context windows and concurrent serving grew. It expanded inference configuration beyond weight quantization into dynamic state management.
The field now combines architectural sharing, quantization, eviction, prefix caching, paging, and tiered storage.
engineering: Start from the cache equation and profile prefill, decode, and transfer separately. Pick a method only after identifying which multiplier or memory tier causes the bottleneck.
Build adversarial long-context evals: exact retrieval at every position, repeated entities, code dependencies, tool history, and long generation. Log which tokens are evicted or quantized.
limits: Eviction and selection can permanently discard evidence. Quantization can perturb attention scores, and custom kernels may erase theoretical gains. Combining lossy methods can fail nonlinearly.
No method guarantees universal long-context quality. Cache policy may need per-request risk levels, with exact retention for regulated or high-value tasks.
connections: MQA/GQA change KV-head count before runtime. PagedAttention manages physical blocks without semantic compression. FlashAttention reduces temporary attention IO rather than persistent cache bytes.
takeaways: KV memory has several independent multipliers.
H2O retains heavy hitters plus recent tokens.
KIVI quantizes keys and values asymmetrically.
SnapKV selects prompt positions from attention observations.
Memory savings and semantic loss must be measured together.
High-risk tasks may require an exact-cache path.

topics.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
topics.authors: Patrick Lewis, Ethan Perez, Aleksandra Piktus, Fabio Petroni, Vladimir Karpukhin, Naman Goyal, Heinrich Küttler, Mike Lewis, Wen-tau Yih, Tim Rocktäschel, Sebastian Riedel, Douwe Kiela
topics.organization: Facebook AI Research, UCL, and New York University

canonicalSources.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks

topics.contribution: Combined a pretrained sequence generator with dense retrieval over an external document index, creating a model with parametric and non-parametric memory.
topics.prerequisites: Encoder-decoder models, dense vector retrieval, maximum inner-product search, and latent variables.
topics.readingLens: The original RAG jointly trains retrieval and generation over Wikipedia passages. Modern pipeline RAG often uses different embedders, chunkers, rerankers, and prompts.
topics.equation: p(y|x) = Σ_z p_retriever(z|x) × p_generator(y|x,z)

problem: Language-model parameters store broad knowledge but are difficult to update, inspect, or cite. Pure generation can produce fluent unsupported facts, while retrieval systems return evidence without composing an answer.
The paper asks whether generation can condition on retrieved documents and learn which evidence helps the task.
coreIdea: Use a dense retriever to select passages from a Wikipedia index and a BART generator to produce the output conditioned on the input plus retrieved text. Treat the selected document as a latent variable and marginalize over top candidates.
RAG-Sequence uses one document for the whole output; RAG-Token can choose a different document distribution for each generated token.
mechanism: Encode the query, retrieve top-k passage vectors with maximum inner product, concatenate each passage with the input, and run the generator. Combine document-conditioned probabilities according to retriever scores.
Train end to end for downstream tasks while keeping the document index fixed in the original setup. At inference, outputs can be traced to retrieved candidates.
technical: The retriever begins from DPR question and passage encoders. Approximate nearest-neighbor search makes millions of passages practical. Marginalization couples retrieval probability with token likelihood.

Modern RAG frequently separates retriever and generator training, adds hybrid search and reranking, and injects passages directly into decoder prompts. Those are descendants, not all claims of this paper.
evidence: The paper reported state-of-the-art results on several open-domain question-answering tasks and generated more factual, specific language than a parametric-only baseline on knowledge-intensive generation.
Wikipedia coverage, answer matching, and benchmark structure constrain the result. Retrieval can return convincing but irrelevant or outdated evidence.
impact: RAG became a dominant architecture for enterprise knowledge assistants because documents can be refreshed without retraining the full model and can support citations.
It split application quality into retrieval, context construction, generation, and attribution, each requiring independent evaluation.
engineering: Evaluate retrieval recall before generation quality. If the required evidence is absent from top-k, prompt changes cannot recover it. Log query, index version, retrieved chunks, reranker scores, and cited spans.
Design permission filtering before retrieval and recheck access at document delivery. Separate “retrieved,” “used,” and “cited” evidence; they are not equivalent.
limits: Retrieval adds latency and can amplify index errors, poisoning, or stale documents. A generator may ignore evidence or cite it without entailment.
Chunking breaks document structure, dense similarity can miss exact constraints, and external memory does not make reasoning or attribution automatically faithful.
connections: BERT-style encoders support dense retrieval. ReAct extends the idea by letting a model decide when to query tools during a trajectory rather than retrieving once at the start.
takeaways: RAG combines parameter memory with an external document index.
Retrieval quality bounds answer quality.
Documents can be updated independently of model weights.
Top-k inclusion is not proof the answer used the evidence.
Permissions and provenance belong in the retrieval path.
Modern RAG is a larger family than the original architecture.

topics.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
topics.authors: Jason Wei, Xuezhi Wang, Dale Schuurmans, Maarten Bosma, Brian Ichter, Fei Xia, Ed Chi, Quoc Le, Denny Zhou

canonicalSources.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models

topics.contribution: Showed that few-shot examples containing intermediate reasoning steps can elicit large language models to solve multi-step arithmetic, commonsense, and symbolic tasks more accurately.
topics.prerequisites: Few-shot prompting, autoregressive decoding, and reasoning benchmarks.
topics.readingLens: A chain of thought is generated text that can improve computation. It is not guaranteed to be a faithful explanation of the model’s internal causal process.
topics.equation: Prompt: question → rationale → answer; test: new question → generated rationale → answer.

problem: Standard prompting asks a model to map a complex question directly to an answer. Multi-step tasks require intermediate variables and decomposition, but the output objective offers little room to compute them.
Earlier rationale methods often required training data or model changes. The paper tests a prompt-only method.
coreIdea: Include worked examples whose outputs contain natural-language reasoning before the final answer. A sufficiently large language model imitates the pattern and generates intermediate steps for a new problem.
Those generated tokens act as a scratchpad, distributing computation across the sequence instead of demanding an immediate answer.
mechanism: Choose representative demonstrations, write concise valid rationales, and format final answers consistently. Append a new question and sample or greedily decode the rationale and answer.
Score the final answer while separately inspecting reasoning errors. Multiple sampled chains can later be aggregated through self-consistency, though that is subsequent work.
technical: The model’s recurrent computation occurs through autoregressive tokens: each generated step becomes context for the next. This increases inference tokens and exposes intermediate text to prompt and decoding choices.
The paper observed strong scale dependence. Small models often produced incoherent chains or failed to benefit, while very large models showed large gains.
evidence: On GSM8K, MultiArith, and other reasoning tasks, chain-of-thought examples substantially improved large-model accuracy; PaLM 540B with the method reached a new result on GSM8K at the time.
The evaluated tasks often have short, checkable answers. Gains and scale thresholds vary by model, prompt, and dataset.
impact: Chain of thought changed prompting from answer formatting into inference-time computation and led to self-consistency, scratchpads, verifier-guided search, tool use, and reasoning-model training.
It also encouraged evaluation of process traces, though later work showed explanations can be plausible without faithfully reflecting why the model answered.
engineering: Use concise demonstrations that match the task and validate final outputs with deterministic tools where possible. Treat generated rationales as untrusted working state.
Measure accuracy against extra tokens, latency, and exposure risk. Hidden or summarized reasoning may be preferable when traces contain sensitive data or misleading explanations.
limits: Chains can confidently contain invalid steps, rationalize an answer after the fact, or copy superficial prompt patterns. More tokens can compound error.
The method does not prove symbolic reasoning or faithful interpretability. Prompt selection and benchmark contamination can inflate results.
connections: Tree of Thoughts adds branching and search over intermediate states. ReAct interleaves reasoning with external actions. Test-Time Scaling formalizes how additional inference compute should be allocated.
takeaways: Intermediate tokens can serve as an inference scratchpad.
Few-shot rationales teach a reasoning format without weight updates.
Benefits were strongly scale-dependent in the paper.
Final answers and reasoning validity need separate checks.
Generated explanations are not guaranteed faithful.
Extra reasoning trades latency and tokens for potential quality.

topics.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models
topics.authors: Shunyu Yao, Dian Yu, Jeffrey Zhao, Izhak Shafran, Thomas L. Griffiths, Yuan Cao, Karthik Narasimhan

canonicalSources.title: Tree of Thoughts: Deliberate Problem Solving with Large Language Models

topics.contribution: Generalized chain-of-thought into explicit search over candidate intermediate states, allowing generation, evaluation, lookahead, and backtracking.
topics.prerequisites: Chain of thought, breadth/depth-first search, heuristic evaluation, and sampling.
topics.readingLens: Tree of Thoughts is a search scaffold around model calls. Quality depends on state representation, branching, evaluator calibration, and compute budget.
topics.equation: Search nodes = partial thoughts; expand with generator; score with evaluator; keep or backtrack.

problem: A single chain commits to each generated step. One early mistake can poison everything downstream, and ordinary decoding offers no deliberate exploration or backtracking.
Classical problem solving searches alternatives and evaluates partial states. The paper brings that structure to language-model reasoning.
coreIdea: Represent a coherent intermediate step as a “thought.” Generate several candidate next thoughts, evaluate their promise with the language model or task rules, and use breadth-first or depth-first search to explore a tree.
The model becomes both proposal mechanism and heuristic evaluator, while an external controller owns search state.
mechanism: Define a task-specific state and thought granularity. Sample candidate continuations. Score partial states independently or through voting, retain the best frontier, and continue until a solution or backtrack condition.
For Game of 24, thoughts are arithmetic steps; for writing, they can be plans. The controller verifies terminal answers where rules permit.
technical: Branch factor, depth, beam width, and evaluation samples determine compute. A coarse thought hides errors; a tiny thought creates an enormous tree.
Using the same model to generate and evaluate is convenient but correlated. Deterministic constraints or separate verifiers improve reliability when available.
evidence: The paper reported large gains over input-output and chain-of-thought prompting on Game of 24, creative writing, and mini crosswords, including a dramatic Game of 24 improvement.
Tasks were selected to demonstrate search and use task-specific controllers. Results do not imply one generic tree prompt solves arbitrary reasoning.
impact: Tree of Thoughts popularized inference orchestration as an algorithmic layer above the model and influenced planner agents, beam reasoning, verifier-guided search, and graph-of-thought variants.
It made the compute-quality frontier explicit: better answers may come from more model calls rather than a larger checkpoint.
engineering: Define serializable state, legal actions, terminal conditions, and deterministic checks before choosing a search algorithm. Cache repeated states and enforce token/call budgets.
Log the complete tree with scores and pruning reasons. Without observability, cost explosions and evaluator mistakes are hard to diagnose.
limits: Search multiplies latency and cost. A weak evaluator can prune the correct branch, and model-generated values may be poorly calibrated.
Many tasks lack compact states or verifiable partial progress. Search over verbose natural language can duplicate semantically identical branches.
connections: Tree of Thoughts branches beyond Chain-of-Thought’s single path. ReAct adds observations from tools. Test-Time Scaling studies adaptive allocation rather than one fixed search budget.
takeaways: A single reasoning chain is one path through a larger possibility space.
Generation and evaluation are separate roles.
Search enables lookahead and backtracking.
Thought granularity controls tree complexity.
Evaluator errors can dominate generator quality.
Budget and trace logging are mandatory in production.

topics.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
topics.authors: Shunyu Yao, Jeffrey Zhao, Dian Yu, Nan Du, Izhak Shafran, Karthik Narasimhan, Yuan Cao

canonicalSources.title: ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models

topics.contribution: Interleaved language-model reasoning traces with external actions and observations, grounding multi-step decisions in tools and environments.
topics.prerequisites: Chain of thought, tool APIs, agent loops, and prompt demonstrations.
topics.readingLens: ReAct is a trajectory format and control loop, not a complete production agent platform. Tools, permissions, recovery, and evaluation remain external responsibilities.
topics.equation: Thought_t → Action_t → Observation_t → Thought_t+1 until Finish.

problem: Chain-of-thought reasoning operates only over model context and can hallucinate facts. Action-only agents interact with environments but may lack a visible plan or accumulated interpretation.
The paper seeks a combined trajectory where reasoning guides information gathering and observations correct reasoning.
coreIdea: Prompt the model with examples that alternate thoughts, tool actions, and returned observations. The model decides whether to reason, call a tool, or finish with an answer.
External evidence enters the next context, creating a feedback loop rather than a one-shot retrieval step.
mechanism: Define a small action grammar such as Search, Lookup, or environment commands. Parse the model’s action, execute it, append the trusted observation, and ask for the next step.
Stop on a valid finish action or budget. Evaluate both final outcome and trajectory behavior.
technical: The environment controller must separate model text from executable action and observations. Parsing, timeouts, retries, and injection resistance are systems concerns outside the language model.
Thought traces help debugging but can contain unsupported assumptions. Observation provenance and tool errors should be explicit rather than blended into assistant prose.
evidence: The paper reported gains on HotpotQA and FEVER through Wikipedia interaction and stronger success on ALFWorld and WebShop compared with imitation or reinforcement-learning baselines in the tested settings.
Tool set, demonstrations, and environment simulators structure the task heavily. Production websites and enterprise tools introduce permissions and nondeterminism not covered by those benchmarks.
impact: ReAct became a foundational pattern for tool-using agents and appears in agent frameworks as an observe-decide-act loop.
It encouraged trajectory-level evaluation and made tool descriptions, action schemas, and observation formatting part of prompt engineering.
engineering: Use typed tool calls rather than parsing free-form strings. Enforce authorization and revalidate consequential arguments at the tool gateway, independent of the model’s prior reasoning.
Set step, token, time, and cost budgets. Record tool requests, normalized results, errors, retries, and final receipts for reproducibility.
limits: The agent can loop, select the wrong tool, trust poisoned observations, or fabricate actions. Reasoning traces do not guarantee correct planning.
Long trajectories consume context and compound failures. High-stakes actions require approval, idempotency, and transactional safeguards beyond ReAct.
connections: RAG retrieves evidence as part of generation; ReAct lets the model choose retrieval or action repeatedly. Tree of Thoughts adds branching, while Test-Time Scaling determines how much inference effort to spend.
takeaways: ReAct interleaves reasoning, action, and observation.
Tools can ground and correct model knowledge.
A controller must mediate every executable action.
Typed schemas are safer than free-form parsing.
Trajectory quality matters beyond final answers.
Budgets, approvals, and receipts are production additions.
